questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement'.

The angry boss asked him to hurry up, [lest he will miss] the important train to the conference.

options.option_text: lest he may miss
lest he should miss
lest he would miss
No improvement (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: In English grammar, the conjunction 'lest' (meaning 'with the intention of preventing' or 'to avoid the risk of') is always followed by the modal verb 'should' or by the base subjunctive verb. Therefore, 'lest he should miss' is the correct substitution.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No required change'.

Whenever she has breakfast, she [prefer to drink] tea rather than coffee in the mornings.

options.option_text: prefer to drinking
preferred drinking
prefers to drink
No required change

questions.explanation: The subject of the sentence is 'she', which is a third-person singular pronoun. Therefore, the verb must also be in its singular form ('prefers'). 'Prefers to drink' fixes the subject-verb agreement error perfectly.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

He is undisputedly [one of the best students who has] ever studied in this prestigious university.

options.option_text: student who have
student who has
No correction needed
students who have

questions.explanation: In the construction 'one of the [plural noun] who...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the immediate antecedent plural noun ('students'), not to 'one'. Therefore, the verb following 'who' must be plural to match 'students'. Thus, 'students who have' is correct.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

[If I was the prime minister], I would definitely eradicate absolute poverty from this country entirely.

options.option_text: If I were the prime minister
If I am the prime minister
If I had been prime minister
No correction required

questions.explanation: The sentence states a hypothetical, unreal, or imaginary condition in the present. In the subjunctive mood, 'were' is used for all subjects, including 'I', 'he', 'she', and 'it'. Thus, 'If I were' is the grammatically correct form.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

Hardly [he had left the house] when it started raining heavily and violently.

options.option_text: he has left the house
did he leave the house
had he left the house
No correction required

questions.explanation: When a sentence begins with a negative adverbial expression like 'Hardly', 'Scarcely', or 'No sooner', it requires subject-verb inversion. The auxiliary verb ('had') must precede the subject ('he'). Thus, 'had he left' is correct.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

The regional manager, along with his entire team of developers, [are working late] tonight to meet the deadline.

options.option_text: have been working late
is working late
were working late
No correction required

questions.explanation: When two subjects are connected by phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', or 'together with', the verb strictly agrees with the first subject. Here, the primary subject is 'The regional manager' (singular), so the singular verb 'is' must be used.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

Scarcely had the exhausted passengers boarded the delayed flight [than the pilot announced] another technical issue.

options.option_text: then the pilot announced
that the pilot announced
No correction required
when the pilot announced

questions.explanation: The adverb 'scarcely' is always paired with the conjunction 'when' to denote that one event happened almost immediately after another. Using 'than' is a common error resulting from confusion with the phrase 'no sooner than'.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

Neither the principal nor the teachers [was present at the annual prize event] at the school.

options.option_text: were present at the annual prize event
was present at the event held that day
are present at the annual prize event
No improvement is required here at all

questions.explanation: With 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (proximity rule). Here 'teachers' is plural and nearest to the verb, so 'were present' is correct. Option B ('was present') wrongly treats the compound subject as singular. Option C ('are present') incorrectly shifts tense to present simple in a past-context sentence.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

By the time we [will reach] the venue, the opening ceremony would have already begun.

options.option_text: will have reached the venue safely
shall reach the venue right there
reach the venue there on time
would reach the venue right there

questions.explanation: In time-adverbial clauses introduced by 'by the time', the future is expressed by the simple present tense, never by 'will'. So bare 'reach' is correct. Option A ('will have reached') doubly errs by placing a future form inside a time clause. Option D ('would reach') inserts a conditional form that is equally invalid in a time subordinate clause.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

The mountaineer is used to [climb] steep peaks in sub-zero weather conditions.

options.option_text: climb steep peaks in such conditions
climbing steep peaks in harsh weather
have climbed steep peaks earlier too
No improvement is required here now

questions.explanation: 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to' and always takes a gerund (verb+ing), not a bare infinitive. So 'climbing' is correct. The common trap is confusing this with 'used to + bare infinitive' (past habit), e.g., 'He used to climb' — a structurally different construction. Option C ('have climbed') is wrong because 'be used to' is not a perfect-tense auxiliary.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

The new electric model is [superior than the previous version] in terms of battery efficiency.

options.option_text: superior to the previous version
more superior than the previous one
superior over the previous version
No improvement is required here at all

questions.explanation: 'Superior' is a Latin-comparative adjective that takes the preposition 'to', never 'than'. 'Superior to' is the only correct standard form. Option B ('more superior than') is doubly wrong: it adds 'more' to an already comparative adjective and pairs it with the wrong preposition. Option C ('superior over') is a common preposition error with no standard backing.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

The geography teacher explained [that the equator divided] the Earth into two equal hemispheres.

options.option_text: that the equator had divided
that the equator was dividing
that the equator would divide
that the equator divides

questions.explanation: Universal or permanent truths retain the present tense in reported speech regardless of the reporting verb's tense. Since the equator always divides the Earth (an unchanging geographic fact), 'divides' (simple present) is correct. Options A and B wrongly apply the sequence-of-tenses rule, which is suspended for scientific and universal truths.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

No sooner [had he arrived at the station when] the last express train pulled away from the platform.

options.option_text: had he arrived at the station than
he had arrived at the station when
did he arrive at the station than
has he arrived at the station than

questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is a fixed correlative pair — 'when' cannot replace 'than'. Additionally, 'No sooner' triggers mandatory subject-auxiliary inversion with past perfect: 'No sooner had he arrived...than'. Option B loses the required inversion. Option C ('did he arrive') uses simple past instead of past perfect, which is obligatory to mark the action as completed just before another. Option D ('has he arrived') wrongly uses present perfect.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement needed'.

The nurse reminded the patient to take medicines [lest the condition will worsen] during the recovery period.

options.option_text: lest the condition would worsen
lest the condition may worsen
lest the condition should worsen
lest the condition might worsen

questions.explanation: 'Lest' is a subjunctive conjunction meaning 'for fear that' and strictly requires 'should + bare infinitive' in the subordinate clause. 'Lest...should worsen' is the only grammatically correct form. Options A ('would') and D ('might') are the most tempting errors — candidates confuse the mandatory subjunctive 'should' with conditional/possibility modals. Option B ('may') is also disallowed; 'lest' never takes 'may', 'will', 'would', or 'might'.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

The news about the train derailment [have spread] to all neighbouring districts by midnight.

options.option_text: has spread to all the neighbouring districts
have spread to all neighbouring districts
had been spreading all across the districts
No improvement is required in the sentence

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'news' is an uncountable singular noun that always takes a singular verb — 'has spread', not 'have spread'. Option C ('had been spreading') incorrectly shifts to past perfect continuous for an event that was completed at a fixed past time (midnight), making simple past or present perfect more appropriate.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

She has been working at this organisation [since five years] and has earned several commendations.

options.option_text: since five long years of her tenure
for the past five years in total
since the last five years back now
No improvement is required in this sentence

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'since' marks a specific point in time (e.g., since 2019), while 'for' marks a duration (e.g., for five years). 'Five years' is a span, so 'for' is mandatory. Option C compounds the error by retaining 'since' and adding the redundant 'back now', a pattern common in Indian English that examiners specifically set as a trap.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

No sooner [the ceremony ended when the guests began] to leave the auditorium in a hurry.

options.option_text: did the ceremony end than the guests began
the ceremony had ended when the guests had
had the ceremony ended that the guests began
No improvement is required in the sentence

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'No sooner' is a negative adverbial that triggers subject-auxiliary inversion and must be followed by 'than', never 'when'. The correct pattern is: No sooner + did + subject + V1 + than. Option C is the most tempting distractor — it correctly inverts the subject ('had the ceremony ended') but uses 'that' instead of 'than', a classic near-miss that SSC examiners regularly set.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

The relief funds were [divided between] the nine affected villages in the flood-prone district.

options.option_text: divided among the nine affected villages
distributed between each of the nine villages
divided between all nine affected villages
No improvement is required in the sentence

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'between' is used when exactly two parties are involved, while 'among' is required for more than two — here there are nine villages. Option B not only retains the incorrect 'between' but also makes 'each of the nine' redundant alongside 'distributed'. Option C similarly keeps 'between' for nine parties, which is the core error left uncorrected.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

The warden announced that the hostel gates [will be locked] at ten o'clock every night without exception.

options.option_text: will be locked at ten o'clock sharp
would be locked at ten o'clock nightly
shall be locked at ten o'clock daily
No improvement is required in this sentence

questions.explanation: B is correct because in reported speech, when the reporting verb ('announced') is in the simple past, the future auxiliary 'will' must backshift to 'would'. Option A retains 'will', ignoring the sequence of tenses rule. Option C uses 'shall', which in formal grammar is reserved for first-person future or strong obligation and is incorrect here for third-person indirect speech.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

The disciplinary panel recommended that the errant official [was transferred] to a remote posting immediately.

options.option_text: is transferred to a remote posting at once
be transferred to a remote posting there
should be transferred to a remote posting
No improvement is required in this sentence

questions.explanation: B is correct because verbs of recommendation, demand, and suggestion (recommend, insist, demand, urge, propose) require the mandative subjunctive in the that-clause — the bare infinitive 'be', irrespective of subject or tense. 'Was transferred' is indicative past and is wrong. Option C ('should be transferred') is the most tempting distractor; though acceptable in informal speech, the formal standard tested in SSC CGL and IBPS PO demands the bare subjunctive 'be transferred', not a modal periphrasis.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

At no point during the inquiry [the finance team disclosed any irregularity] in the accounts they maintained.

options.option_text: the finance team had disclosed any lapse
did the finance team disclose any finding
was the finance team disclosing any fact
No improvement is required in this sentence

questions.explanation: B is correct because placing a negative or restrictive adverbial phrase ('At no point') at the front of a sentence mandates subject-auxiliary inversion: did + subject + bare infinitive. The original has no inversion at all. Option C attempts inversion using 'was...disclosing' (past progressive), which is syntactically inverted but semantically wrong — it implies an ongoing, interrupted attempt at disclosure rather than the completed non-disclosure that the sentence intends.
